items.sourceTitle: US unveils sanctions on ICC in move court condemns as 'assault on rule of law'

source_propositions.source_text: The Trump administration has unveiled sweeping sanctions on the International Criminal Court (ICC) in a significant acceleration of its attempt to "dismantle" what it sees as a "rogue" institution.

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the measures - which include a ban on US entities making transactions with the ICC - were intended to "defend US sovereignty" and accused the court of seeking to prosecute Americans.
The ICC said the measures were an assault on the rule of law and the foundations of the international legal order.
The announcement came just hours after former ICC judge Navi Pillay was awarded the 2026 Nobel Peace Prize for her efforts to promote peace and international law.
The US has already sanctioned 17 of the ICC's judges and officials, but this move sanctions the court itself as an institution and is intended to collapse its ability to operate financially.

However, the US has provided a six month grace period before some of these latest sanctions kick in, meaning member states can keep paying for its operations - a move Washington says is to allow countries time to negotiate a "solution to address" US concerns.
UN Secretary General Antonio Guterres called the US decision "a serious blow to our collective pursuit of international criminal justice, of which the ICC is a key pillar".

The UK joined Canada, Denmark, Germany, France, Italy, Japan and the Netherlands in reaffirming their "continued and unwavering support" for the ICC and said they "regret and strongly disagree with" the sanctions.
They also praised the court's staff for their work bringing "those accused of the most serious international crimes to justice", as well as supporting victims.
The ICC was founded in 2002 to prosecute war crimes, crimes against humanity and genocide, and counts 125 countries as member states.
Several major countries remain outside the ICC, including the US, Russia, China, India and Israel.
The Trump administration argues the ICC is run by what it calls globalists who threaten American sovereignty.

HONG KONG (AP) — The top trade envoys for China and the European Union agreed Friday on a broad initial deal following two days of talks aimed at calming escalating tensions over trade imbalances, the EU trade commissioner said.

Neither side provided clear details on the preliminary deal, but European Commissioner for Trade Maros Sefcovic said it includes lower tariffs for some European goods to China as well as measures to stabilize rare earth supply chains.
The EU trade envoy said the deal could cut up to 50% of Chinese electric and plug-in hybrid vehicle imports to the EU and could lower tariffs on products benefiting “almost every” EU nation.
The deal would require approval from leaders across the 27-nation EU.
He said that “by this step we are actually preventing several millions of car exports from China to the European Union.”
The two sides were seeking to resolve key factors behind China’s growing trade surplus, which hit 360 billion euros ($403 billion) last year.
China’s Commerce Ministry posted online that Chinese Commerce Minister Wang Wentao expressed concerns about the EU’s recent restrictive measures.
He said that China is not the root of the EU’s problems but a partner in solving them.

The head of the European Automobile Manufacturers’ Association, Sigrid de Vries, said that the deal appears to avert further instability in the EU and “can help facilitate the transition to a new era of Chinese presence in the European market in an orderly way and this is in the long-term interests of all parties.”
Sefcovic said he will brief EU leaders meeting in Brussels next week and seek their approval.
“They would have to see that this is convincing enough to take the other steps,” he said.

“We are in a situation that they (China) could put under the threat whole sectors in the European industry, literally thousands of jobs and the public opinion and the leaders clearly expect very fast action from our side.”

source_propositions.source_text: A key piece of the Carney government's economic agenda, Bill C-39, passed its first vote in the House of Commons on Thursday, with Conservatives and the majority Liberals sending the bill for study by a special committee.
The 243-page bill proposes to extend the government's approach to major infrastructure projects to other projects across the country.
The government wants those projects to undergo one review instead of several reviews, and to have that single review completed within one year.
The legislation is a core part of the Liberals' plans to pivot the economy away from reliance on the United States and present Canada as a reliable trading partner to overseas markets.

Before the vote, Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre said his party would support sending the legislation to committee in order to propose amendments to what he called a "weak, watered-down, long-delayed" bill.
Poilievre told reporters he wants the government to speed up the decision timeline on projects to between six months and a year, and to add measures to protect workers' rights.
Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre says his party will be proposing amendments to Bill C-39.
(Justin Tang/The Canadian Press) He also said Conservatives would seek to eliminate the industrial carbon price and create "shovel-ready zones" with pre-permitting for developments.
Prime Minister Mark Carney's government will use a special committee formed to study the sweeping legislation.
The 11-member committee includes MPs from the Liberals, Conservatives and Bloc Québécois, with the Liberals holding a majority of seats.
It doesn't include representation from the NDP, which does not have official party status in the House of Commons, a requirement for automatic inclusion on standing committees.

NDP House leader Don Davies said he asked the government to allow his party to participate in the committee but Government House leader Steven MacKinnon turned him down, a move Davies called "fundamentally undemocratic."

The Chittagong Port Authority (CPA) and global port operator DP World today (8 October) signed a 15-year concession agreement to operate and modernise the New Mooring Container Terminal (NCT) and its Overflow Container Yard, bringing one of the world's largest port operators into Bangladesh's main container terminal.

CPA Chairman Rear Admiral Md Moniruzzaman and DP World Chairman Essa Kazim signed the agreement at the Invest Bangladesh auditorium in Dhaka in the presence of Shipping Minister Shaikh Rabiul Alam, State Minister for Shipping Md Rajib Ahsan, and UAE Ambassador to Bangladesh Abdulla Ali Al Hamoudi, among others.
Essa Kazim also led a delegation at a meeting with Prime Minister Tarique Rahman today to discuss expanding trade and investment between Bangladesh and DP World.
Tarique sought an update on DP World's interest in establishing free trade zones and rail-based inland container depots in Bangladesh, as well as making new investments in the country.
NCT handled about 13.85 lakh TEUs last fiscal year, accounting for roughly 44% of Chattogram Port's total container handling.

Under the concession, DP World will operate, maintain and modernise NCT, while the CPA will retain ownership of the terminal, land and infrastructure, as well as regulatory oversight and overall control.
The government has highlighted around $150 million in investment and other commitments over 15 years, higher CPA revenue, modern equipment, automation and faster cargo handling as key benefits.

However, the full concession agreement has not been made public, including detailed investment obligations, performance benchmarks, revenue-sharing terms, worker protections, maintenance requirements and termination conditions, raising questions over how key commitments will be measured and enforced.
Rabiul Alam said DP World would start work within six months of signing and begin full-fledged operations within two years.
DP World will make an upfront payment of around Tk600 crore to CPA, with 25% payable upon signing and 75% before operations begin.

It will invest more than Tk1,000 crore in the first 10 years, while the broader package includes about $150 million in investment and other commitments, including around $90 million for equipment, technology and upgrades.
CPA earned Tk6,629 crore in FY26 by handling 3.52 million TEUs.

(Nikkei montage/Source photos by Getty Images) DHAKA -- Bangladesh signed a 15-year deal with DP World on Thursday for the Dubai-based logistics company to operate and maintain the New Mooring Container Terminal (NCT) at the country's largest port, ending years of negotiations over one of the country's most politically sensitive infrastructure projects.

The Chittagong Port Authority (CPA) and global port operator DP World on October 8, 2026 (8 October) signed a 15-year concession agreement to operate and modernise the New Mooring Container Terminal (NCT) and its Overflow Container Yard, bringing one of the world's largest port operators into Bangladesh's main container terminal.

CPA Chairman Rear Admiral Md Moniruzzaman and DP World Chairman Essa Kazim signed the agreement at the Invest Bangladesh auditorium in Dhaka in the presence of Shipping Minister Shaikh Rabiul Alam, State Minister for Shipping Md Rajib Ahsan, and UAE Ambassador to Bangladesh Abdulla Ali Al Hamoudi, among others.
Essa Kazim also led a delegation at a meeting with Prime Minister Tarique Rahman on October 8, 2026 to discuss expanding trade and investment between Bangladesh and DP World.
Tarique sought an update on DP World's interest in establishing free trade zones and rail-based inland container depots in Bangladesh, as well as making new investments in the country.
NCT handled about 13.85 lakh TEUs last fiscal year, accounting for roughly 44% of Chattogram Port's total container handling.

Under the concession, DP World will operate, maintain and modernise NCT, while the CPA will retain ownership of the terminal, land and infrastructure, as well as regulatory oversight and overall control.
The government has highlighted around $150 million in investment and other commitments over 15 years, higher CPA revenue, modern equipment, automation and faster cargo handling as key benefits.

However, the full concession agreement has not been made public, including detailed investment obligations, performance benchmarks, revenue-sharing terms, worker protections, maintenance requirements and termination conditions, raising questions over how key commitments will be measured and enforced.
Rabiul Alam said DP World would start work within six months of signing and begin full-fledged operations within two years.
DP World will make an upfront payment of around Tk600 crore to CPA, with 25% payable upon signing and 75% before operations begin.

It will invest more than Tk1,000 crore in the first 10 years, while the broader package includes about $150 million in investment and other commitments, including around $90 million for equipment, technology and upgrades.
CPA earned Tk6,629 crore in FY26 by handling 3.52 million TEUs.

items.sourceTitle: ICE has quietly used this warehouse as a detention facility all summer, neighbors say

source_propositions.source_text: A Roxbury, N.J., warehouse was one piece of a billion-dollar plan by the Department of Homeland Security to detain migrants.
Alvarado Jr. for NPR hide caption ROXBURY, N.J. — On a warm morning on Sept. 4, masked immigration agents rolled into Dover, N.J.

Footage of the raids rippled across social media, sent people into hiding and reignited rumors that had been circulating for months: Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents were taking people to a nearby warehouse.
The warehouse in Roxbury was one piece of a billion-dollar plan by the Department of Homeland Security to detain migrants as part of President Trump's mass deportation efforts.
That plan to convert warehouses into detention centers faced fierce backlash and legal challenges from residents and immigrant advocates.

It was largely abandoned, and in several sites, including Roxbury, the government is legally forbidden by a court order from converting them to a detention facility, pending environmental assessments.
But an NPR investigation has found signs that the New Jersey facility is being used.
And the state's Office of the Attorney General says it is looking into similar reports.
In early 2026, Homeland Security bought 11 warehouses to turn into ICE detention facilities.
They spent about a billion dollars on these.
NPR spoke to an official at a government contractor whose company was approached to convert several of the warehouses into ICE facilities.
He spoke on the condition of anonymity for fear of retaliation from the government.

items.sourceTitle: How Science, Indigenous Knowledge, and Sea Otters Are Restoring Canada’s Kelp Forests - The Daily Goods

source_propositions.source_text: A stretch of ocean in Clayoquot Sound is being turned into a kelp nursery, as a First Nation, a restoration group and a kelp company try to rebuild an ecosystem under pressure.

The partnership between the Tla-o-qui-aht First Nation, Redd Fish Restoration Society and West Coast Kelp has planted more than 4,200 square metres of new kelp habitat since launching in early 2026 in the traditional territory of the Tla-o-qui-aht First Nation.
“We have grown a lot of kelp,” Emily Fulton, marine program manager for the nonprofit Redd Fish Restoration Society, told Mongabay in a phone interview.
Organisers describe it as the largest kelp restoration project on the West Coast of North America.
The team is growing baby bull kelp and giant kelp on four lines, each 330 metres long, suspended below the water’s surface and away from seafloor predators such as sea urchins.
As the kelp matures, some of it will be removed from the lines and transplanted to sites across Clayoquot Sound to restore degraded kelp forests and seed new ones.

The project has cost almost a quarter of a million Canadian dollars, with funding from sources including the provincial government, the World Wildlife Fund of Canada and the Clayoquot Biosphere Trust.
For Saya Masso, natural resources manager for the Tla-o-qui-aht, the work is tied to restoring what his community once had.
“A society that thrived on the West Coast for 10,000 years, we lived under a system of abundance,” he told Mongabay in a phone interview.
Fulton said the project is also about preparing before kelp loss becomes worse in Clayoquot Sound.
“If and when that happens, we just have to be ready to act rather than, at that point, go, ‘now how do we do it,” she said.
Scientists estimate 11,542 square kilometres of kelp forest are lost globally every year.

items.sourceTitle: The girls in the Gaza school photograph

source_propositions.source_text: Just before the genocide, 15 Gaza schoolgirls posed for a photograph.
Three years on, Al Jazeera went looking for them.
Nuseirat, Gaza Strip — Maha Taha fills the old blackboard with equations and sets her students to work.
For the next few minutes, the classroom settles into the scratch of pens and the low murmur of girls working through the problems.
Maha, 43, has taught mathematics for 20 years.
Dressed in an olive-green jalabeya and beige hijab, she steps quietly to her desk at the side of the room, as her students work through the maths problems.
She has watched generations of girls pass through her classroom, preparing for exams and applying to universities.
Asked about the girls she taught before the October 7 genocide began, Maha pauses before reaching for her phone.
While scrolling back to find a photograph taken in June 2023, she speaks softly, so as not to disturb the girls in the classroom.

“I was proud of them," she says. "I could see that they had bright futures ahead of them. They were very special in their personalities, even before it came to their studies. But October 7 changed the course of their lives.”
In the photo, 15 teenage girls in navy school robes and white scarves crowd around Maha in the schoolyard.
Some have their arms around one another; others lean towards the camera.

Nature volume 658 , pages 327–336 ( 2026 ) Cite this article Dozens of independent origins of multicellularity have profoundly shaped Earth’s evolutionary and ecological history.
These transitions have given rise to massive radiations encompassing thousands to millions of species and the evolution of increasingly complex bodies.
Multicellular taxa now constitute the majority of Earth’s biomass and have fundamentally transformed global ecosystems, underpinning diverse biomes from forests and grasslands to coral reefs.
While these macroevolutionary patterns have long been recognized, the microevolutionary processes driving the transition to multicellularity have remained unclear.

Questions remain on how solitary cells form cohesive groups, how these groups become evolutionary units capable of adaptation at the multicellular level, and how novel cell types and developmental patterns emerge.
Recent discoveries of previously unknown multicellular species and the development of experimental models have provided important insights into these questions.

This work reveals that seemingly insurmountable evolutionary hurdles are often readily overcome either through the repurposing of ancestral unicellular traits or through emergent properties of multicellular collectives that arise spontaneously.

Here we review key breakthroughs in our understanding of the microevolutionary processes that underpin the evolution of increasingly complex multicellularity, focusing on mechanisms through which single cells can evolve into functionally integrated multicellular organisms.

items.sourceTitle: UChicago scientists reveal a Jurassic otter that could chew and swallow like modern mammals

source_propositions.source_text: A well-preserved fossil of a 165-million-year-old mammal ancestor from China with hind limbs like a platypus and a broad, flattened tail like a river otter appears to be one of the oldest such creatures adapted for swimming and hunting in the water.

Dubbed Megacauda sungei (meaning “big tail”) , the Jurassic mammaliaform also shows the earliest evidence yet of bony structures of the throat that gave this mammal predecessor the ability to feed and swallow like modern mammals—thought to lead to the diversification of mammal species with a wide variety of diets.

“This is an incredibly important evolutionary innovation. After mammals chew their food, be it plants or meat, they all swallow it in the same efficient and effortless way,” said Zhe-Xi Luo, the Mila Pierce-Rhoads Professor of Organismal Biology and Anatomy at the University of Chicago and senior author of a new study describing the fossil in Nature .

“Once early mammals had this apparatus, each group could develop specialized teeth and diversify into a tremendous range of food resources. They could be carnivores, insectivores, herbivores, omnivores, or anywhere in between.”
All modern mammals, including humans, have hyoid bones that link the mouth and throat passage down to the esophagus and the larynx.
They are arranged in a U-shaped saddle, suspended by a chain of bony segments to the skull.
This helps adult mammals to use throat muscles to swallow chewed food one lump at a time, instead of gulping down huge bites or whole prey like an alligator.
These structures also give babies the ability to suckle mother’s milk.
Megacauda is from an extinct lineage of “docodonts,” which are near relatives of mammals from the Mesozoic Era.
In 2019, Luo and his colleagues discovered a tiny docodont from around the same geological age called Microdocodon gracilis , which also had mammal-like hyoid bones.
Megacauda is a much bigger animal, though—40 to 50 centimeters long and weighing one to two kilograms.
It also has better preservation than other fossils of the delicate bony structures underneath the skull for suspending the palatal and pharyngeal muscles.
